concept.name: Marking the close
concept.definition: A manipulative or disruptive trading practice whereby a trader buys or sells a large number of futures contracts during the closing period of a contract — the period in which the settlement price is determined — in order to benefit an even larger position in an option, swap, or other derivative that is cash-settled based on that day's settlement price.
concept.intuition: You shove the price around in the last minutes of trading not because you want the position, but because today's official closing price sets the payoff on a much bigger bet you hold elsewhere.
concept.mechanics: The trader concentrates aggressive orders in the closing window to push the settlement print up or down. A derivatives position sized much larger than the closing-period trades then settles off the distorted price, so a small loss on the closing trades is outweighed by the gain on the larger position.
concept.failure_modes: Heavy closing-period volume is also produced by legitimate index rebalancing, MOC orders, and delta-hedging; proving manipulation requires showing the trading was intended to distort the settlement price rather than to fill a genuine need at the close.
concept.misconceptions: Trading large size at the close is not inherently abusive; the violation lies in trading specifically to engineer the settlement price for the benefit of a related position.
concept.example: A fund short 50,000 cash-settled gas swaps sells 2,000 futures contracts aggressively in the final two minutes of the settlement window, depressing the settlement price by 3 cents and increasing the swap position's value far more than the cost of the futures sales.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary — A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
